 Answer Man: Duke’s downtown substation location? Why can’t we vote in any precinct on Election Day? 
 by 
 JOHN BOYLE 
 November 16, 2026

 Duke Energy is building a new substation to service downtown on a site on Rankin Avenue behind the Harrah's Cherokee Center-Asheville. // Watchdog photo by John Boyle
 Today’s round of questions, my smart-aleck replies and the real answers:
 Question: I have a couple questions regarding Duke Energy’s new substation behind Harrah’s Cherokee Center Asheville. Why couldn’t this station be rebuilt where the old one was instead of getting relocated to a site that was formerly parking for Harrah’s staff. Also, there was a protest when an earlier proposed location between Rankin and Lexington avenues drew objections over tree removal. What about the trees that were removed from the new site? Are the trees at one location more special than those at another?
 My answer: All trees are special, sir, and they all deserve a big hug. Except for holly trees, maybe. That’s a bad idea. Or those with poison ivy vines wrapped all around them.
 Real answer: The new substation is under construction on Rankin Avenue, right behind the Harrah’s Cherokee Center. 
 Duke Energy spokesperson Zach Vavricka answered on behalf of the company.
 Sign up for free Watchdog news alerts straight to your inbox.
 Yes! Sign me up! 
 “The Rankin Avenue substation is more than 50 years old, and rebuilding it is an important investment in the reliability and resiliency of the electric system serving downtown Asheville,” Vavricka said via email. “As the Asheville area has grown over the past two decades, so have its energy needs, and these improvements will help ensure we can continue providing reliable electricity to homes and businesses while increasing capacity to serve the community’s future needs.”
 Vavricka said Duke worked closely with the city throughout the site selection and design process.
 “After hearing community concerns about vegetation removal and the loss of public parking associated with the original proposal between Rankin and Lexington avenues, Duke Energy and the city worked together to identify the parcel adjacent to the existing substation at Rankin Avenue and Hiawassee Street as an alternative,” Vavricka said. “The revised location went through an extensive public and regulatory review process.”
 The previous parcel did not provide enough room to safely maintain or quickly replace critical equipment, he added.
 Duke Energy provided this rendering of what a new substation on Rankin Avenue will look like. // Provided by Duke Energy 
 “The new design gives crews the space they need to perform maintenance and respond more efficiently if equipment fails, helping limit the duration of potential customer outages while keeping the overall footprint as small as practical,” Vavricka said. 
 To safely build the substation, “minimal vegetation clearing is necessary,” he noted, adding that the work is consistent with approved plans and permits.
 “Duke Energy has developed a vegetation plan that incorporates native plants designed to complement the surrounding downtown environment,” Vavricka said.
 Duke and the city restarted work on a new substation location near Harrah’s in January 2023.
 City of Asheville spokesperson Samantha Booth said the city and Duke both achieved objectives with the new Rankin Avenue location. The city’s webpage on the project notes that in August 2022, the city and Duke temporarily paused the project to consider options and get community input.
 “Rather than a ‘tradeoff,’ the land exchange and partnership allowed for mutual goals to be met,” Booth said via email. “The city was able to support the critical community need for reliable electricity while maintaining priorities for the city, such as minimizing the number of trees removed and maximizing the opportunity for maintenance and/or renovation of the Harrah’s Cherokee Center Asheville.”
 Question: If voters can easily vote early at any available location, why is this same option — voting at any precinct in your county — unavailable on Election Day?
 My answer: I’ll answer that in a minute, but am I the only one who misses the daily deluge of campaign flyers in my mailbox? Kinda made me feel important for a few months, you know?
 Real answer: Buncombe County spokesperson Lillian Govus said the short answer is that state law requires it to be done this way. 
 But it’s also a practical matter, in practice coming down to equipment and ballots.
 “During early voting, we use ExpressVote machines, which allow us to electronically access the correct ballot for voters,” Govus said. “If you were one of the 97,000 people who voted early in Buncombe County, you used this electronic marking machine.”
 The East Asheville Library was an early voting site this year. // Watchdog photo by Katie Linsky Shaw 
 Buncombe County had 32 different ballot types this election because voters were deciding races for County Board of Commissioners, Asheville City Council, Buncombe County Schools, Town of Black Mountain, and more, Govus said.
 “We do not use ExpressVote machines on Election Day,” Govus said. “Vote centers, similar to how early voting works, are not allowed on Election Day in North Carolina.”
 If you were one of the 30,000 people who voted on Election Day, Govus said, you received a pre-printed ballot specific to your geographic region.
 “Each ExpressVote ballot marking device costs around $4,000, so it’s financially challenging to have them for 80 Election Day polling locations,” Govus continued. “Likewise, it’s not financially or environmentally responsible to print all 32 ballots to have on hand at 80 polling locations on Election Day.”
 The state Board of Elections issued a memo that outlines how many printed ballots the county must have on hand.
 “We’re a hybrid county, so that means we must order pre-printed ballots at least equal to 60 percent of the number of registered voters in the county corresponding to each ballot style,” Govus said.
